explanations.explanation: Jerusalem it is, friend. Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar's father and the earlier king of Babylon, took those vessels from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem (Daniel 5:3). These weren't just fancy cups. They came from God's house, and that matters for everything coming next.

Samaria is a real place, but it never shows up in this story. The text says the vessels came from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem (Daniel 5:3). Mixing them up is like grabbing the wrong set of keys on the way out the door. Happens to the best of us, and I once spent an hour looking for a spatula I was holding.

Shiloh isn't in this passage at all, friend. The vessels were taken from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem (Daniel 5:3). Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar's father, is the one who took them. So the answer is Jerusalem, and now you've got it in your pocket.

explanations.answer: So they can drink from them
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says Belshazzar gave the order “so that the king could drink from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, wanted vessels from God's house as party cups. The text also says he gave the order under the influence of the wine, and I think that tells you how the evening is going.

explanations.answer: So they can be sent back
explanations.explanation: Nope, nobody is mailing anything back to Jerusalem tonight. The text says the vessels were brought in so the king could drink from them. Belshazzar, king of Babylon, gave that order under the influence of the wine. These cups were headed for the party, not for the road home.

explanations.answer: So they can be melted down
explanations.explanation: Melting them down would be a plan, but it's not THIS plan. The text says Belshazzar, king of Babylon, wanted the vessels so that the king could drink from them with his nobles, his wives and his concubines. He gave that order under the influence of the wine. The vessels went straight from the shelf to the cups.

True. The text says that as they drank the wine, “they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.” They were doing it with vessels from the house of God in Jerusalem. Keep that picture in your head, because Daniel talks about it later (Daniel 5:23).

It's actually True, friend. The text says that as they drank the wine, “they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.” That's the list: six materials, and every one of them a thing somebody made. Belshazzar and his guests were doing this while drinking from vessels taken from God's house.

explanations.answer: His face grows pale and his knees knock together
explanations.explanation: Yes! The text says “his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.” A moment ago, Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was the life of the party. Then a hand started writing on his wall, and the party was OVER.

explanations.answer: He laughs and lifts his cup toward the hand
explanations.explanation: No laughing in this room, friend. The text says his face grew pale and his knees knocked together. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, had just been the loudest one at the feast. Now he's the one who can't stand up straight.

explanations.answer: He jumps up and shouts for his palace guards
explanations.explanation: Jumping up would take working legs, and his hips gave way. The text says his face grew pale and his knees knocked together. He does call out, but it's for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners (Daniel 5:7), not for guards. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was frozen first and shouting second.

That's right. The text says the king called for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners, and it names them “these wise men of Babylon.” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, went straight to the experts he already had. You'd call your own experts first too.

The prophets of Baal show up in a different story, with Elijah on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:19). Elijah was a prophet of the LORD in Israel. Here, the text says Belshazzar called for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners, “these wise men of Babylon.” So it's a Babylon crowd tonight.

The elders of Israel aren't in this room, friend. The text says Belshazzar, Babylon's king, called for the enchanters, astrologers and diviners, “these wise men of Babylon.” He hadn't even thought of anyone from outside his own court yet. Somebody will have to speak up for him.

explanations.answer: Neither read it nor interpret it
explanations.explanation: Right, they got NOTHING. The text says all the king's wise men came in, “but they could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” That's all of them, not just a couple. I think a thousand nobles watching that happen is a whole lot of quiet.

explanations.answer: Read it but not interpret it
explanations.explanation: Close, but they couldn't even get that far. The text says the wise men “could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” They couldn't read it, so they had nothing to interpret. The king's whole team of experts hit a wall, and I mean that literally.

explanations.answer: Interpret it but not read it
explanations.explanation: That would be a neat trick, friend, explaining something you can't even read. The text says the wise men “could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.” They came up empty on both. Reading comes first, and they didn't get past it.

It's actually False. The text says “King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.” When his wise men couldn't help, the king didn't calm down. He got worse, and so did the mood in the room.

That's right, False. The text says that after the wise men came up empty, “King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.” He was already scared, and now he's scared on top of scared. Nobody in that hall had a good idea yet.

Yes! The queen says, “Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.” Nebuchadnezzar is Belshazzar's father, the king who took the temple vessels. She reminds Belshazzar that his own father had trusted this man.

Cyrus, king of Persia, shows up in other places (Ezra 1:1), but he's not the one here. The queen says, “Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.” Nebuchadnezzar was Belshazzar's father and king of Babylon before him.

Ahasuerus, the king in the book of Esther (Esther 1:1), belongs to a different story. Here the queen tells Belshazzar, “Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners.” So the king who picked this man was Belshazzar's own father.

That's what she says. The queen tells him, “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” She has a lot of confidence in this man, and she says it plainly to the king. Her advice is simple: send for Daniel.

explanations.answer: Copy the writing onto a scroll
explanations.explanation: Nobody says anything about copying in this scene, friend. The queen says, “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” The king wants the writing explained, not saved for later. A copy of something you can't read is just a copy of a mystery.

The wise men have already been and gone, and they couldn't help (Daniel 5:8). The queen sends Belshazzar a different direction: “Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.” She says this about one man, and she doesn't suggest bringing more experts.

Actually, False. Daniel tells the king, “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else.” Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, doesn't reach for the purple or the gold chain. He still goes on to read the writing for the king.

That's right. Daniel, one of the exiles from Judah, says to the king, “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else.” The purple and the gold chain were on the table, and Daniel pushed them back across it. Plenty of people would've said yes, friend.

explanations.answer: Read the inscription and interpret it
explanations.explanation: Yes. Daniel says, “Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.” He turns down the gifts, but he doesn't turn down the job. Both things are in the same breath.

explanations.answer: Pray for the king through the night
explanations.explanation: That's not what the text says. Daniel tells the king, “Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.” The text doesn't mention praying through the night. What Daniel promises is a reading and an interpretation.

explanations.answer: Ask his God to erase the writing
explanations.explanation: Nobody asks for the writing to be erased. Daniel says, “Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.” The writing stays on the wall, and Daniel explains it. An erased wall wouldn't give the king any answers, friend.

explanations.answer: He was deposed from his throne
explanations.explanation: That's it. Daniel says that when Nebuchadnezzar's heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, “he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.” Daniel is telling this to Nebuchadnezzar's son, Belshazzar, so he's reminding the king of his own family's history. Pride cost Nebuchadnezzar a lot.

More conquering isn't what happened. Daniel says that when Nebuchadnezzar's heart became arrogant, “he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.” His glory went DOWN, not up. This is the king Belshazzar is hearing about from Daniel.

explanations.answer: He built a new royal palace
explanations.explanation: No new palace in this part of the story, friend. Daniel says that when Nebuchadnezzar's heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, “he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.” Nebuchadnezzar lost the throne instead of gaining a building.

It's actually False. Daniel says to Belshazzar, “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.” So Belshazzar DID know what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. That's what makes the charge so heavy.

That's right. Daniel tells Belshazzar, “But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.” Belshazzar knew his father's story. He heard it, and he still didn't humble his heart.

explanations.answer: He holds the king's very breath in His hand
explanations.explanation: Right. Daniel describes Him as “the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.” That's the true God, the one Belshazzar didn't glorify. The gods Belshazzar praised “cannot see or hear or understand,” and the God Daniel names holds the king's breath.

explanations.answer: He leaves the king to rule his own ways
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Daniel says. He describes God as the One “who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.” The king's ways are in God's hand, not out of it. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was ruling on borrowed breath.

explanations.answer: He shares His glory with the gods of gold
explanations.explanation: Daniel says nothing like that. He calls those gods ones that “cannot see or hear or understand.” Then he describes the true God as the One “who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.” Gods that can't see or hear aren't sharing anything.

It's actually False. Daniel says to Belshazzar, “Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.” The “He” is the Lord of heaven, the God Belshazzar didn't glorify (Daniel 5:23). The gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone didn't send a thing, because they “cannot see or hear or understand.”

That's right, False. Daniel says, “Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.” He is talking about the Lord of heaven, whom Belshazzar did not glorify (Daniel 5:23). The writing didn't come from the gods Belshazzar praised.

explanations.answer: God has numbered the days of his reign
explanations.explanation: Yes. Daniel says, “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.” It's the first word on the wall, and it's a short one. Belshazzar's reign had an ending, and the word said so.

explanations.answer: God has forgiven the pride of the king
explanations.explanation: That's not what Daniel says. He tells the king, “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.” That's a message about the end of a reign, not about forgiveness. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, had to hear it straight.

explanations.answer: God will add more years to his reign
explanations.explanation: More years isn't in the message, friend. Daniel says, “MENE means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.” The days were numbered and the reign was done. The word was about finishing, not adding.

That's the word. Daniel says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” Belshazzar was weighed, and he came up short. That's a hard thing to hear, so Daniel says it plainly.

Faithful would be a nicer word, but it's not the one on the card. Daniel says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was weighed and came up short. That's the message Daniel read out.

Worthy would've sounded better, but Daniel doesn't say it. He says, “TEKEL means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” The scales didn't favor Belshazzar, Babylon's king. The word is deficient.

Yes, the Medes. Daniel says, “PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” That's the third part of the message, and it's about the kingdom itself. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, was hearing that his kingdom was going to someone else.

Egyptians aren't in this message, friend. Daniel says, “PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” So the kingdom is going to the Medes and Persians. Nobody from Egypt is mentioned.

The Assyrians aren't named here. Daniel says, “PERES means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.” That's the answer for the blank. Belshazzar, Babylon's king, heard it from Daniel's own mouth.

True. The text says, “Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom.” Belshazzar had just heard that his reign was ending, and he kept his promise anyway. I think that's a king keeping his word on a very strange night.

It's actually True. The text says, “Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom.” Even after hearing about the end of his reign, Belshazzar gave the command. Daniel had said to keep the gifts, and the king gave them anyway.
Yes! The text says, “Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” It happened the very night Belshazzar was slain, right after Daniel read PERES. That's the message coming true.

Hiram, king of Tyre, belongs to Solomon's day (1 Kings 5:1), not to this story. The text says, “Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” Tyre never comes up here. Darius took the kingdom the night Belshazzar was slain.

Sennacherib, king of Assyria, is in a different part of the Bible (2 Kings 18:13). The text here says, “Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.” That's the man who took Belshazzar's kingdom. Assyria isn't part of this night at all.
